title: Operator Handbook Synthesis from Chaos Week — Compact Action Playbook
author: Marcus Chen
content:
Summary

This retrospective distills the operational learnings from 'Chaos Week 2026' into a compact, prioritized set of handbook changes, decision heuristics, and runnable playbooks. The goal is to convert observed failure modes and operator improvisations into durable procedures so that future operators can resolve similar incidents reliably and faster.

Background

In 2026-01-08 through 2026-01-10 we ran a focused chaos campaign across platform services (batching layer, kv-prefix cache, tenant router, and model-variant fallback). The exercise intentionally injected degraded network conditions, slow kernels, and simulated preemption. Operators exercised their existing handbooks and created ad-hoc mitigations. This document synthesizes what worked, what failed, and the minimal actionable changes to the operator handbook and observability surface.

Scope and intended readers

- Primary: Platform operators and oncall engineers owning runtime/allocator/traffic-shaping.
- Secondary: Platform product managers, SRE leads, and devs who author runbooks.

Key findings (top-level)

1) Operators often relied on a single mental model for eviction vs. degrade: prefer a two-stage decision canvas (evict vs degrade).
2) Alert context lacked token-cost and tenant-priority signals; operators spent 12–18 minutes per incident assembling them manually.
3) Cross-service fallback logic (model swap -> tenant fallback) had unclear owner and rollback instructions.
4) Several ad-hoc CLI commands used during the exercise are safe and should be formalized; two were unsafe and removed.
5) Runbook prose was too verbose for high-severity incidents; a one-page "Incident Action Card" per runbook speeds triage.

Concrete metrics observed

- Median time-to-first-action (operator) during Chaos Week: 9m 40s (target: <5m).
- Median resolution time for degraded kv-prefix cache scenarios: 43m (target: <30m).
- Operators queried token-cost and tenant-priority signals manually in 78% of incidents.
- 3 unsafe mitigation commands were executed once (no production impact but high risk).

Synthesis: Where to change the handbook now (top 5 prioritized changes)

1) Add a standardized Incident Action Card (IAC) template to every runbook.
   - What it is: a single page checklist with the first 6 diagnostic steps, immediate mitigations, and safe-rollbacks.
   - When to use: SEV2/SEV1 for runtime services.

2) Introduce a Two-Stage Decision Canvas for eviction vs degrade.
   - Stage A: Fast eligibility checks (is tenant critical, SLO burn rate, warmset heat).
   - Stage B: Operator mitigation choices (soft-evict, reduce tokens per request, model-variant swap).

3) Create a small telemetry bundle that surfaces token-cost and tenant-priority in alert context.
   - Implementation: enrich alert payloads with three fields: tenant_priority (high|medium|low), recent_1m_token_rate, 1h_budget_spend_pct.

4) Formalize and publish safe CLI primitives and deprecate unsafe ones.

5) Define ownership and rollback clauses for model-variant fallback logic across runtime and routing teams.

Incident Action Card (IAC) — template (to be added to runbooks)

- Title: [Service] — IAC — [Scenario]
- Severity: [SEV1|SEV2]
- Immediate diagnosis (first 6 checks, < 4 minutes):
  1) Confirm alert signature and scope: alert_id, affected_regions, affected_models.
  2) Query operator context panel: tenant_priority, token_rate_1m, slot_utilization.
  3) Run healthcheck summary: curl -sS https://ops-api.internal/health/service/[svc] | jq '.summary'.
  4) Verify KV cache hit ratio and prefix shard errors: kvestats --service [svc] --window 5m.
  5) Check kernel wait and GPU utilization: gpu-proc top --json | jq '[.gpus[] | {util, mem}]'.
  6) Capture and pin the current model-variant routing snapshot: rroute snapshot create --note \"chaos-injection\"
- Immediate mitigations (ordered):
  a) Set temporary tenant throttle: rquota set --tenant $TENANT --rate 0.5 --expire 15m  # safe throttle
  b) Engage soft-eviction on warmset: opsctl warmset evict --shard $SHARD --fraction 0.2
  c) If token-cost spike > 250% and tenant_priority=low, apply auto-buydown credit: billing-adm credit-apply --tenant $TENANT --amt 0.
- Safe rollback steps: reverse mitigations in reverse order. Document timestamps to audit.

Runbook change table (summary of edits)

| Runbook | Edit type | Owner | ETA |
|---------|-----------|-------|-----|
| kv-prefix-cache | add IAC + safe CLI list + telemetry enrichment | runtime-team | 2026-03-15 |
| tenant-router | add Decision Canvas + rollback clauses | platform-routing | 2026-03-22 |
| model-variant-fallback | clarify cross-team ownership + canned rollback | serving-runtime | 2026-03-10 |
| operator-oncall-playbook | shorten SEV path to 1 page + training checklist | eng-sre | 2026-03-08 |

(Above table is a compact summary; full change diffs are linked in related_pages.)

Example alert enrichment payload (pseudo-JSON)

{ "alert_id": "ALRT-2026-00073", "service": "kv-prefix-cache", "region": "us-west-2", "context": { "tenant_priority": "low", "recent_1m_token_rate": "4500/tokens", "1h_budget_spend_pct": "68%" } }

Note: keep enrichment payload under 2KB to avoid alerting pipeline amplification.

Operator heuristics (codified)

- Heuristic 1: If tenant_priority == high AND 1h_budget_spend_pct < 85% AND kv_hit_ratio > 40% then prefer graceful degrade (reduce token window) over eviction.
- Heuristic 2: If kernel wait > 80% and GPU memory pressure > 90% then trigger model-variant swap to a quantized variant (preview models allowed only in dedicated namespaces).
- Heuristic 3: If multiple tenants show simultaneous SLO burn with correlated token spikes, prioritize by tenant_priority and apply soft-throttles starting from low priority tenants.

Safe CLI primitives (approved)

1) rquota set --tenant <id> --rate <float> --expire <duration>  # throttles tenant traffic safely (idempotent)
2) opsctl warmset evict --shard <id> --fraction <0.0-1.0>  # controlled warmset eviction
3) rroute snapshot create --note <string>  # capture routing state (write-only snapshot)
4) backend-rollout pause --component <comp> --reason <string>  # soft pause for automated rollouts

Unsafe commands observed (deprecated)

- runtime-force-evict --shard X --all  # performs immediate full shard eviction, caused cascading cold starts in the exercise. Remove from operator path and place in engineering-only tooling.

Training and verification plan

1) Update runbooks and IAC templates (owners listed in table) — owners must submit PR with edits by ETA.
2) Publish a 60-minute microtraining for operators covering: Decision Canvas, IAC usage, and approved CLI list (target date: 2026-03-29).
3) Run a focused tabletop in the next gameday (April 2026) with 3 injected scenarios derived from Chaos Week. Each scenario must include a measurable median time-to-first-action target.

Roadmap alignment and follow-ups (how this maps to platform roadmap)

- Q2 2026: Telemetry enrichment rollout and alert-payload schema v1 (owner: observability).
- Q2 2026: Runbook consolidation sprint (owner: eng-platform runbook guild).
- Q3 2026: Automation for frequent safe mitigations (owner: eng-platform/operator-automation).

Action items (owner/accountability)

1) runtime-team: Draft runbook IAC and safe CLI list PR — due 2026-03-15. (owner: Priya Menon)
2) observability: Implement alert enrichment fields and test with synthetic alerts — due 2026-04-05. (owner: Elena Rivera)
3) platform-routing: Add Decision Canvas and rollback clauses to tenant-router runbook — due 2026-03-22. (owner: Jamal Ortiz)
4) eng-sre: Schedule and run 60-minute microtraining and April tabletop — schedule by 2026-03-20. (owner: Marcus Chen)
5) security: Review CLI primitives for privilege hardening — due 2026-03-10. (owner: Serena Gupta)

Appendix A — Short cookbook for triage (command snippets)

1) Quick health summary (single-liner):
   curl -sS https://ops-api.internal/health/service/kv-prefix-cache | jq '.summary // \"unknown\"'
2) Capture routing snapshot:
   rroute snapshot create --note \"triage-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)\"
3) Apply a safe throttle to tenant 42 for 10 minutes at 0.4 RPS:
   rquota set --tenant 42 --rate 0.4 --expire 10m

Appendix B — Postmortem checklist for converting ad-hoc fixes into handbook text

1) Was the action repeatable and low-risk? If yes, add as a Safe CLI primitive.
2) Did the action require cross-team approvals? If yes, document the ownership and rollback clause.
3) Can the action be automated? If yes, create a follow-up ticket to build and test automation.
4) Add IAC references and sample alert contexts to the runbook.

Closing note

Chaos Week revealed that small edits to the operator handbook and a compact incident action card can reduce cognitive load and shave 4–12 minutes off median time-to-first-action. The prioritized edits above are intentionally conservative: they convert observed safe operator behavior into repeatable processes while deferring heavier automation until telemetry enrichment and rollback guarantees exist.

If you have questions, objections, or additional observations from the exercise, add comments to this page or file a follow-up ticket in the runbook guild backlog (label: runbook-updates).
